cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Super Straight Road

Tau has a long East-West road that is difficult to line up.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Coconut / No Powerline

Tau has a long East-West road that is difficult to line up.

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and you see a lot of Coconut Palms, you're in the central part of the road, east of the river.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Coconut / Powerline / No Guardrail

Tau has a long East-West road that is difficult to line up.

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and you see a lot of Coconut Palms, you're in the central part of the road, east of the river.

On this stretch, if you have a powerline, but no guardrail, you're east of the river, and west of the small sideroad on the map.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Concrete / Overgrown / Guardrail / No Powerline

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and a lot of overgrowth between you and the coast, you're generally in the Western Part of the road.

If additionally, you have a guardrail, but no powerline, you're on the east-west stretch west of the river.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Concrete / Overgrown / No Guardrail

Tau has a long East-West road that is difficult to line up.

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and a lot of overgrowth between you and the coast, you're generally in the Western Part of the road.

If additionally, you have no guardrail, you're on the stretch marked on the second image, south of a smooth coast protrusion west of the river.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Overgrown - Powerline
cards.note:
Tau has a long East-West road that is difficult to line up.

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and a lot of overgrowth between you and the coast, you're generally in the Western Part of the road.

If additionally, you have a powerline visible, you're on the SW-NE stretch immediately west of the river.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Visible Coast / Guardrail

Tau has a long East-West road that is difficult to line up.

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and you have the coast North of you, with no significant vegetation in the way, you're on the Easternmost part of the road, east of the little sideroad.

The western half of this stretch has a guardrail, the eastern half does not.

cards.a: American Samoa - Infrastructure - Tau - Visible Coast / No Guardrail

If you're generally heading East-West, have Concrete Pavement and you have the coast North of you, with no significant vegetation in the way, you're on the Easternmost part of the road, east of the little sideroad.

The western half of this stretch has a guardrail, the eastern half does not.

This taxi with the white body, blue roof and blue logo is unique to the city of Bariloche.

cards.a: Argentina - Infrastructure - La Pampa Junction Sign

La Plata has white taxis with green elements.
Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.

Taxis in Neuquen are all yellow. What distinguishes them from Cordoba taxis is that their doors have no logos or paintings on them.
Taxis with a red-white-green stripe (hungarian flag) are unique to Resistencia.

Red taxis with a black stripe are unique to Salta.
White taxis with a yellow roof are unique to San Juan.
White taxis with two light-blue stripes (resembling the Argentinian flag) are unique to San Luis.

cards.a: Argentina - Infrastructure - Santiago del Estero Taxi

In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.
White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.
These old-school, white taxis with a yellow-black checkerboard stripe are unique to Tucuman.
The ∀-Poletop is found in South Australia and New South Wales. In SA, the pole will be a stobie pole, while in NSW it will be round.
Within Australia, a speed limit of 130 km/h can only be found in the Northern Territory.
South Australia is the only Australian state that uses a 25 speed limit in school zones.
Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.
Unique to Australian Capital Territory (Canberra).

This black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - Blue Square on Pole

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - bollard with brown bottom

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - bollard with short reflector

Identified by the little symbol.

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - Charters Towers Red Roads

According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.
The city of Darwin, NT uses concrete shelters as bus stops.
Dorat Road (23) in the Northern Territory can be easily recognized thanks to its distinct Darwin area landscape and lack of road lines.
These round concrete poles with dots going up on them are found in New South Wales.
Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are flat rather than round.
Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost exclusively found in Queensland.
This street sign is unique to Gold Coast City Council.

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - Green Dot on Pole

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - hydrant with blue circle

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - hydrant with red top

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - License Plate - Slim NSW

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - License Plate - Slim Victoria

In addition, a unique white truck with a snorkel, and cab guard can be found.

Octagonal Poles in Australia are found mostly in and around Sydney.

New South Wales is the only state to use red ‘No Stopping’ signs.

cards.a: Australia - Infrastructure - South Australia Bus Stop

On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as Blue Coast), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

NOTE: Blue infrastructure can be found to a lesser extent all across France, particularly Brittany, so consider the landscape as well.

In the outskirts of Bordeaux, you may find square traffic signposts with the Bordeaux shade of red, named after the wine grown in the region.

NOTE: Red posts by themselves are not unique to Bordeaux, so apply this meta with caution.
Small tables with 'Arrᵗ' written on a small separate sign, are found in Bordeaux, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.

Road signs where both the post and back are painted brown are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is square, however round signposts are equally common.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the name of the city, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a modern design, and many city names will be river based, notably named after Seine and Marne.

NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.

Cuboid barriers made of stones and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape.

NOTE: Stone barriers with a rounded top are not found on Corsica.

Dark green road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.
Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a green sticker, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.

cards.a: France - Infrastructure - Grey Signback / Green Signpost
cards.note:
A greyish green signback supported by a darker green post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.
Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.

Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.

NOTE: Outside Lyon proper, the street sign will display the name of the suburb instead.
Marseille’s street signs will usually feature the city’s emblem, a variation of the Greek cross. The white border will usually be interrupted at the top, even when the cross is absent.
Montpellier street signs will typically contain a blue ‘M’ on a white background in the top left corner.

Paris uses an iconic green & Prussian blue design with a top arch that has also been replicated in Bucharest, which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.

NOTE: The simple rectangular form of the sign can be found in the towns nearby and rarely in other cities.

In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a dark green post paired with a signback of a lighter shade of green, ranging from matcha green to greenish turquoise. The department’s logo, a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present on the signback.

NOTE: Under certain lighting, they can appear similar to the greyish road signs. Also, beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.
Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

Roads with a significant red, purple or burgundy tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of Burgundy, which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area.

NOTE: Normal roads may deceptively look reddish under some lighting, so use this with caution.

Thin B type guardrail, typical for Czechia and Slovakia, is sometimes found on highways in the northern half of the country, often coming from Le Mans, Tours, Paris, Reims and Metz.

NOTE: On the highlighted sections, thin B can be the minority guardrail, and short sections of any highway will have no guardrails at all. It is also more common on smaller roads in the North, but less consistent as a clue.
Wind turbines are considerably more common in the north of the country.

The transformers in Kanto, which can have three or two insulators, are often mounted on a wooden plate and two bars, or a round plate and a T-shaped bar.

cards.a: Japan - Infrastructure - Transformer - Black Tap Connector
cards.note: The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted yellow numbers and black “tap” connectors, are either attached with large triangle and horizontal bars, or these thin metal brackets.
The transformers in Chugoku, which have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a full triangle, will have a long horizontal or short vertical insulator(s) at the end.
The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a half triangle, will have “hat shaped” short horizontal insulators at the end.
These grey “insulator-esque” blocks, which wires are fed through, can be found in the regions of Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and very rarely in Hokkaido.
The transformers in Kyushu, which have a straight bar attached on the side of the pole with three insulators at the end, will have transformers mounted 180-degrees from one another.

The transformers in Hokuriku, which are attached with thin metal bars, often have these small “lamp” shaped insulators. There will never be a bar present except for the attachment mentioned above.

NOTE: The prefecture of Niigata will have the Tohoku transformer design, as opposed to Hokuriku one.
The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted yellow numbers and black “tap” connectors, are either attached with large triangle and horizontal bars, or these thin metal brackets.
Transformers in Okinawa, which have a T-shaped bar attached on the side of the pole, will have transformers mounted on opposite sides of the pole.

The electrical poles in Hokkaido either have this plus-shaped bar attached to the side of the pole, or one transformer mounted on two bars.
In Chugoku, a white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with red numbers. They may also be painted on the side.

This lamp with five circular bulbs that looks like a dice is found in Cancun.
Taxis in and around Mexico City have a white lower half with a pink upper half.

Poles with a lowered crossbar and a single support beam that extend from one end of the crossbar to the pole itself can be found in Durango.

This pavement consisting of hexagonal tiles is found in Puebla and Tlaxcala.
Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text ‘Jalisco’ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.
These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.
This lamp with a rectangular head and a ring-shaped light bulb is found in Matamoros.
Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.
Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.

This lamp with a zig-zag bent pole arm is found in Hermosillo.

You can find this specific design of green fire hydrants in Bergen.

Black plastic snowpoles are more regional and will mostly be found in Trøndelag, Møre og Romsdal and Vestland, but can also be found in Nordland and more rarely in Innlandet, Buskerud, Rogaland and Telemark

Rusty guardrails are almost exclusively found in coastal regions, and particularly on the southern half of the west coast.

Green plastic snowpoles are found mostly around the island of Senja in Troms since the company selling these is also located there. The company also sells other colors less frequently. These can also less commonly be found all over Troms and Finnmark.
Small blue snowpoles can be found around Elverum.
Two red stripes going around lamp posts are commonly found in Stavanger.
Small, wide black pole plates, with a single line of letters and digits, can be found in southeastern Norway.

Street signs in Bursa are green, and generally have slightly extruded letters, meaning the signs are not completely flat.

NOTE: Several other types of infrastructure in Bursa, such as fences and guardrails, may also be coloured green.

Red street signs with a coloured bottom strip are found in several cities. In the bottom right corner, you can find a white arrow and some numbers. If this arrow is pointing in both directions and has a single arrowhead, rather than double, then you are almost certainly in Istanbul.

Beware that simple arrows pointing in only one direction can be found in both Istanbul and in other cities. However, if you see such signs in combination with red house numbers, then you should be in Istanbul.
Street signs in the Izmir Province are dark blue, noticeably bulge outwards and very commonly have the emblem of Izmir in white at the top of the sign.

cards.a: Turkey - Infrastructure - Watertank - Horizontal on top of Vertical
cards.note: Horizontal water tanks placed on top of vertical water tanks are primarily found in a line following the south coast and going up to Elâzığ.
Square water tanks with angled corners are found in the south, approximately from İskenderun to Sanliurfa.
White spherical water tanks can be found in the southeast, mainly south of Batman.
Vertical water tanks can be found in most of Turkey, but are notably uncommon along the south and west coast.

This bollard has a white rectangular plate, with 6 bolts: 2 at the top, 2 in the middle and 2 at the bottom. There are different variants, with circular reflectors, rectangular reflectors, or no reflectors at all.

They're all found in California

Most states have unique, distinct and learnable Adopt-a-Highway signs, which can be seen on the side of roads. A map of those can be seen here. Keep in mind, some states have slight variations in design.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Arrow Street Number
cards.note:
North Carolina commonly uses a style of street signs showing street numbers and arrows in addition to the street name.

NOTE: Other states occasionally feature street signs with similar designs, so use other clues before guessing.
These green ATV Route signs are unique to Wisconsin.
Billboards are banned in Maine, Vermont, Alaska and Hawaii. So if you see one, you can rule those out.
A black stripe can sometimes be seen in between the two yellow, middle road lines in California.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Black/White Overpass Support
cards.note: These stripes on an overpass support are a dead giveaway that it’s South Carolina. Sometimes a sign with yellow and black stripes is used instead

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - California Bridge Marker
cards.note: California posts these bridge markers (with a lot of numbers) on bridges. The county abbreviations used on the bridge markers are different from those on the postal markers.
Utility poles in California usually have markings at the bottom of the pole that consist of 3 yellow stripes.
The city of Chattanooga in Tennessee has its own unique font that is used on some signs in the city.
West Virginia sometimes features street signs with a symbol that resembles a fraction inside a circle.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Clearance on Overpass
cards.note: South Carolina is the only southeastern state to post the clearance on every overpass.

Concrete paving on main highways is much more common in Iowa than in other states.

NOTE: Concrete paving on residential streets is commonly seen throughout the Midwest states and parts of the East Coast.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - County Road - Clark County
cards.note: Clark County is the county Las Vegas is situated in and it uses a unique county route shield.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Dark Wooden Fences
cards.note:
Dark-coloured wooden fences with several horizontal wooden supports are common in farming areas of central and southern Appalachia, stretching from Pennsylvania to Georgia.

NOTE: These types of fences can be found elsewhere to a lesser extent, so use other clues before guessing.

The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a dark metal post with a white diamond on each side of the top.

NOTE: These bollards can be found to a lesser extent in other western states.

Signs attached to two signposts can be seen in Michigan. Not all signs are attached to two signposts.

NOTE: Double signposts can also be seen in other states, but are not as common.
In New Hampshire there will often be a white metal sign with the characters ‘E-2’ on it adjacent to the road, typically at either end of bridges.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Exit Ramp / No Parking
cards.note: Georgia likes to decorate its freeway offramps with no parking signs.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Exit with Speed Limit
cards.note: New Alabama coverage can have these combined exit/speed limit signs.
This bollard is found in Florida.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Green Overpass Marker
cards.note: Overpass bridges in Mississippi have green plaques with white numbers on them.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Green US Route
cards.note: This green U.S. Route shield with the word business at the top is unique to Maryland.
This sign is Illinois-specific.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Green/Red Bridge Marker
cards.note:
Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts use small green and red rectangular signs to mark the ends of bridges and guardrails.

NOTE: Not all bridges and guardrails in these states will have these markers.
Snowplowable raised pavement markers can only be found on highways in the eastern states shown in the image. They are built into the road and somewhat resemble the letter H.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Hanging Yellow Boxes
cards.note:
Many large intersections in Michigan have stop lights and signs that hang from wires that stretch across the middle of the intersection. These markers are commonly in yellow boxes.

NOTE: These are not completely unique to Michigan, but are most commonly seen there.

Maximum speed limits vary by state and territory. The maximum speed limits shown here will generally be seen on interstate highways. Some interstates and highways in their respective states or territories will have lower maximum speed limits than what is shown.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Horizontal Traffic Light
cards.note: Horizontal Traffic Lights are common in Nebraska, New Mexico, Texas and Louisiana. They also appear occasionally in Oklahoma, Louisiana and Georgia.
Signs warning about ice (like this) are commonplace in Louisiana.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Indiana Blue Square
cards.note: This kind of blue square on a post is exclusive to Indiana.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Kansas Sign Reflectors
cards.note: These white reflectors on signposts are unique to Kansas. They are most commonly seen on ‘stop’ signs in rural areas.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Kentucky Rumble Strips
cards.note: Some roads and highways in the state of Kentucky use uniquely-shaped rumble strips that are thin, relatively long recessed lines on the very outside edges of the road.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Key West Poles
cards.note: Poles on Intersections in Key West have a white paint at the bottom which contains the name of the street its on.

Interstate 19 in Arizona from Tucson to the Mexico border uses kilometres on the exit and distance signs. This is the only part of the country that uses kilometres instead of miles for highway signs.

NOTE: Speed limit signs in this area still use MPH instead of KPH.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Large Center Line Gap
cards.note:
Yellow lines with a noticeably larger gap in between them are most common in Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oregon. They can also be found to a lesser extent in Washington, Alabama, and Michigan.

NOTE: Wide middle lines can also rarely appear in other states, so consider other clues before guessing.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Letter Highway Sign (with County)
cards.note: Wisconsin and Missouri are the only two states that use a lettering system (A - ZZZ) for their county highways. Wisconsin signs typically have the word ‘county’ above the letter, while Missouri signs typically do not. The borders of the signs also vary slightly.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Letter Highway Sign (without County)
cards.note: Wisconsin and Missouri are the only two states that use a lettering system (A - ZZZ) for their county highways. Wisconsin signs typically have the word ‘county’ above the letter, while Missouri signs typically do not. The borders of the signs also vary slightly.

Texas’s nickname is the Lone Star State. You can see the Texas star on the state’s flag. Many Texans use the star as a decoration on gates, for example.

Maine often uses a dashed single yellow line or a combination of dashed and solid instead of a solid double one in the middle of a road. I feel like Maine does it a bit more often than other states in the region.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Maryland Overpass Code
cards.note: Some Interstate bridges in Maryland (but not the neighboring states or DC) seem to have this code painted on them. (Discovered by bagaboiebailey in the USA GeoGuessr Community server).

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Midwest Grainy Roads
cards.note: Some rural roads in the Upper Midwest use a similar road pavement to Texas. They will have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’-like road surface, but will vary in colour. These roads are most common in the state of Illinois.
California doesn’t use mile markers.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Minnesota Bridge Sign
cards.note: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Minnesota Stop Sign
cards.note: On most rural ‘stop’ signposts in Minnesota, a black-and-white marker is attached to the posts horizontally. The shape may vary slightly.
Nashville has trash bins with the recognizable logo.

Guardrails, signs, and signposts are commonly painted a medium brown colour in US National Parks, which are often located in the west. Guardrails that are painted brown can be made out of both wood and metal. Rock walls can also sometimes be seen in place of guardrails.

NOTE: There are occasional exceptions to this rule, so consider other clues before guessing in a National Park.
This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Nevada Mile Marker
cards.note: Top part has the highway name. The middle part is an abbreviation of the county name. The lower part has the mile number.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - New Hampshire Interstate Sign
cards.note: These signs should only be found in NH (notice the dividing line between the two numbers).

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - New Hampshire US Route Sign
cards.note: These are also specific to New Hampshire. Notice the dividing line on the sign.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - New Jersey - 500 Series County Routes
cards.note: These county routes are given unique three-digit numbers that begin with a 5. There is only one route per number. The same number cannot be duplicated in multiple counties. There is therefore only one County Route 525 in the entire state of New Jersey. What’s also interesting about the 500 Series routes is that they follow the same cardinal direction rule as Interstates: even-numbered routes run east-to-west and odd-numbered ones north-to-south. In common with the U.S. Routes, the numbers increase southward.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - New Orleans Circle
cards.note: This circular windshield sticker is found in New Orleans, Louisiana.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - No Middle Line
cards.note:
Some small roads in California lack a middle yellow line; instead only feature solid white lines on each side of the road.

NOTE: This can rarely be seen in other states.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - North Carolina - Circular Pay to Park
cards.note: Raleigh, NC uses circular pay to park signs to indicate parking meter locations. (unlike Charlotte, NC)

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - North Carolina / Blue Parking Sign
cards.note: Charlotte uses green parking signs, whereas Raleigh uses blue parking signs.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - North Carolina / Green Parking Sign
cards.note: Charlotte uses green parking signs, whereas Raleigh uses blue parking signs.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - North Carolina / Streetcar
cards.note: Charlotte has a streetcar system unlike Raleigh.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - North Carolina Signpost
cards.note: White signs attached to signposts can commonly be seen in North Carolina.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Number + Direction Road
cards.note:
Streets in Utah and Idaho, particularly in urban areas, are often named by using a combination of a number and cardinal direction (i.e. ‘600 South.’)

NOTE: This style of street naming can be found rarely in other Western states.
Oakland has this tree on their street name signs.

Oil pumpjacks are short, industrial-looking metal structures located at the surface of oil fields and are used to pump crude oil from the earth below. They are most common in western states, particularly in Texas, Eastern New Mexico, and North Dakota.
In Oklahoma, you can often find a green rectangular sign with 3 rows of numbers attached to the back of stop signs at rural intersections
In Alabama, overpasses have these mile markers hanging from them.

Louisiana doesn’t call its counties counties but uses the word parish instead. This is a relic of the French colonial past of the state. You might occasionally spot the word on an intersection sign, for example. The location is guaranteed to be in Louisiana because no other state uses the word parish in that way.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Pennsylvania Intersection Signs
cards.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen attached to signposts at intersections in Pennsylvania. On top, the number of the converging state route is written.
Alabama likes to glue these stripes to overpass support pillars.

Many bridges are used to connect the various neighbourhoods of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. These expansive, steel bridges are commonly painted bright yellow. Additionally, Pittsburgh is easy to identify because of it being flanked by 3 rivers and steep bluffs on all sides.
These circular reflectors are found in Pittsburgh.
Instead of Mile Markers, California uses postal markers that are white instead of green and have a county abbreviation.

A horizontal blue, red, or green sign can commonly be seen at the ends of driveways in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula. The house number is present, in addition to either the town name and or the road name (usually.)

NOTE: Nearby states often use similar markers, but typically lack any town or street name information and only feature numbers.
These rectangular raised pavement markers are found in the south and west of the US and also in Massachusetts.
Mesa, a city next to Phoenix, sometimes uses these red street name signs in the western part of the city.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Roadname on Sidewalk
cards.note:
In San Francisco, CA, almost every intersection has the road name written on the sidewalk.

This is due to the many earthquakes in this city, making sure every road is still labeled in case the streetsigns fall off.

In rural areas of Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire, short rock walls are commonly visible adjacent to the road.

NOTE: These rock walls can be found rarely in adjacent states.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Small Circle Bollard
cards.note: Roadside bollards in Wyoming often feature a dark metal pole with a white circular reflector at the top. The top of the metal pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to Wyoming.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Small Green Signs
cards.note:
Vermont features small rectangular green signs on stop sign posts with three rows of horizontal numbers. The top row of numbers correlates to the highway or road number that the road with the stop sign intersects with.

The State of New York uses similar style signs. However, these signs can be attached to different types of sign posts (town entry signs, highway signs, etc.)

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - South Carolina Intersection Signs
cards.note: Black street signs with white text can commonly be found at intersections in South Carolina.
Speed signs in Oregon often simply have the word ‘Speed’ instead of the standard ‘Speed Limit’.

Square guardrails are the most dominant (but not the only) type of guardrail in the states of New York and Wyoming. They have a long bar across the top, with several square legs supporting them.

NOTE: These guardrails can be found, to a lesser extent, in some adjacent states.

cards.note: Each of the 50 states has its own state flag. These appear frequently enough that they are worth learning.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - State Flag - North Carolina

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Tennessee Mile Marker
cards.note: Tennessee state routes have these unique mile markers. The larger number is the mile (resets at county borders) and the smaller bottom one is the state route number.
This three-star symbol is found in many places in Tennessee, including but not limited to these historical place signs. It’s the same symbol as on the state flag but it can also be black and white.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Texas - Fully Black Traffic Light
cards.note: Within Texas, completely black traffic lights can be found in Dallas and Houston

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Texas - Fully Yellow Traffic Light
cards.note: Within Texas, fully yellow traffic lights can be found in San Antonio, El Paso and Austin.

Yellow or red bands can commonly be seen around signposts in Texas.

NOTE: Similar reflectors can sometimes be seen in other states, such as Hawaii.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Texas Grainy Roads
cards.note:
Texan roads often have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’-like road surface.

NOTE: Similar pavement can sometimes be seen in adjacent states such as New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Colorado.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Thick Black / Thinner Yellow Sign
cards.note: The black stripes on these signs are a bit thicker in Louisiana than in other states.

Some roads in West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland use middle yellow lines that are thicker than traditional yellow road lines.

NOTE: These are not present on all roads in these states, and can be found elsewhere, so use this tip in conjunction with other clues.

The Greater Miami area has a so-called trolley system which is a free public transport system. Different towns have different colors in their trolleys. The Miami Trolley is orange at the top and green at the bottom, with a small white stripe in between (the colors of the Miami-Dade flag, which are the same as the Indian flag).

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Trolley - Miami Beach
cards.note: The Greater Miami area has a so-called trolley system which is a free public transport system. Different towns have different colors in their trolleys. The Miami Beach Trolley is blue.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Vertical House Number
cards.note:
Properties in rural and exurban Ohio, Lower Michigan, and Indiana commonly feature a vertically-oriented metal sign with white numbers, indicating the house number of the adjacent building. These signs are most commonly blue or green, and are commonly attached to mailboxes.

NOTE: These may be rarely found in other states.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Virginia Intersection Signs
cards.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen at intersections in Virginia.
The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.

Waymo is an autonomous driving company which offers taxi services in several cities. Its cars are very distinct, have a lidar on top and notably have no person sitting behind the wheel. cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - White-Orange Pole Plate

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - DC
cards.note: Cars registered in DC are legally required to have this sticker in their windshield.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - Louisiana

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - Maine

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - New Hampshire
cards.note: Number in a white rectangle with a thick colorful border.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - New Hampshire (old)

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - New Jersey
cards.note: Three rectangles. Each contains a number. The outer ones make a year (like 2023), and are filled in a given color. The central one has a white background and a single digit.

cards.a: United States - Infrastructure - Windshield Sticker - New York
